promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Oct 18 2026, target under 3:45.

new.headline: You ran 3:50, 12 minutes faster than your first marathon, and you ran race week exactly as planned. This week is all recovery: walk first, then run short and easy only once stairs feel normal.

flags.title: Quad recovery
flags.detail: Stairs should feel normal before your first run. If Thursday's 2 mi feels stiff or awkward, stop and walk the rest.

flags.title: Left toe blister
flags.detail: Run in the Brooks Ghost, not the race shoe. Skip a run if the blister changes how you run.

flags.title: Sleep
flags.detail: You averaged 6.5 hours, with one 5-hour night. Aim for 7.5 hours or more, because sleep does most of the repair this week.

flags.title: Easy heart rate
flags.detail: Your easy runs usually sit near 138. If it runs 5 or more beats higher at easy effort, take an extra rest day.

flags.title: What comes next
flags.detail: In your next check-in, tell me whether the Thanksgiving 10K is a race or a fun run, and what your next big goal is.

answers.question: How long before I can run again? A friend wants me to race the Thanksgiving 10K in five weeks.
answers.answer:
Start running again once stairs feel normal and you can walk without stiffness. For most runners that is 4 to 6 days after a marathon. The plan has a 2 mi test run on Thu Oct 22. If your quads still complain, walk that day and try again Saturday. Keep everything easy for two full weeks before any faster running.

The Thanksgiving 10K on Thu Nov 26 fits, as long as it is a bonus and not a goal race. That gives you two weeks to recover, then about three weeks of normal running with strides and one short faster session a week. Your marathon fitness will carry over, so a solid run is realistic, but expect your speed to feel a bit rusty.

Racing it hard and running it alongside your friend need different training from Nov 2. Tell me which one you want in your next check-in, along with your next big goal.

new.analysis:
## Race week went to plan
You ran every planned run at the planned distance, and the rest days stayed rest days. Wednesday's marathon-pace reps averaged 8:34/mi with heart rate topping out at 159, a sign the taper had left you fresh. The spike in total effort and the low share of easy running both come from the race itself, not from doing too much.

## How the race went
You ran a little ahead of goal pace for 20 miles, then lost about a minute per mile over the last 10K.

| Stretch | Pace |
| --- | --- |
| Needed for 3:45 | 8:35/mi |
| First 20 mi | about 8:31/mi |
| Last 10K | about 9:28/mi |
| Whole race | 8:48/mi |

Those first 20 miles were steady and controlled, which is a real skill. The fade came from your legs, not from poor pacing.

## Why the quads gave out
Your legs ran out of durability before your fitness did. The earlier race date left you one 20-miler and a 46 mi peak week, built up from about 30 mi a week. The course also climbed 617 ft, more than any of your long runs, and downhills are hardest on the quads.

Your race-day heart rate tells part of the story. At 8:30/mi in training your heart rate sat around 145 to 153, but on race day it started near 158 and climbed to 164. Hills, nerves and conditions likely made goal pace cost more than training suggested, so you used up your reserves faster.

## What to change next time
The fix for your next marathon is more endurance in your legs, not more speed. A longer build with peak weeks closer to 50 mi would help. So would two or three long runs of 20 to 22 mi, with marathon-pace stretches inside some of them, plus a few hilly long runs to prepare your quads for a course like this one.

## Why this week is so gentle
A marathon damages your muscles, and they keep repairing for a couple of weeks after the soreness fades. Walking early gets blood moving through your legs without the pounding of running. Even if you feel great by Sunday, hold off on faster running until the second easy week is done.

## Looking ahead
Next week, Oct 26 – Nov 1, stays easy, with a little more running and maybe a few relaxed strides at the end if your legs feel fresh.

safetyCallouts.title: Look after the toe blister.
safetyCallouts.body: Keep it clean and covered, and see a doctor if redness spreads or it gets hot, swollen or starts to drain.

safetyCallouts.title: Soreness should ease each day.
safetyCallouts.body: If one spot hurts more than the rest or the pain gets worse, stop running and see a doctor or physio. Do the same if you notice very dark urine or unusual swelling.
